title: Wind Pollination, Fertilization, and Seed Set
objective: Trace pollen from release through stigma contact, fertilization, embryo development, and mature achene formation.

terms.definition: A tube grown by a germinating pollen grain to deliver sperm cells to the ovule.
Fusion of male and female gametes.
Successful development of seeds or achenes following pollination and fertilization.

coreScience: Cannabis is primarily wind-pollinated. Staminate flowers release numerous small pollen grains that can move through air and settle on receptive stigmas. Dispersal is not the same as successful fertilization: pollen must be viable, reach a receptive stigma, hydrate, germinate, and grow a pollen tube to the ovule.

After fertilization, the embryo and seed tissues develop while the ovary matures into the one-seeded fruit unit commonly called a seed. Seed maturation takes time; a darkening exterior alone does not prove complete embryo maturity or high vigor. Parent health, timing, environment, and seed position can influence development and harvest uniformity.

Unplanned pollination changes the production objective. A controlled cannabis study found that fertilization following pollination altered cannabinoid and terpenoid accumulation in the tested genotypes and conditions while resources shifted toward seed development. The magnitude is not universal: genotype, pollination timing, flower position, and production system matter. Controlled breeding therefore requires both a positive identity system for intended parents and a negative contamination-control system for every other pollen source.
cultivationRelevance: Pollen control includes space, timing, airflow, surfaces, clothing, tools, plant movement, and records. Removing a male after visible release does not remove pollen already distributed.
For controlled pollination, label the treated branch and protect unpollinated controls. Record pollen parent, recipient, date, method, and containment.

measureAndRecord.requirement: Plant ID, lineage, collection date, and storage history.
Plant and branch ID, flower stage, and stigma condition.
Isolation, bagging or enclosure, airflow, clothing, and cleanup.
Count, maturity classes, physical defects, and germination test.

misconceptions: Any pollen contact guarantees seed: Viability, stigma receptivity, environment, and fertilization success all matter.
Pollen cannot travel far indoors: Air movement and personnel can distribute pollen beyond the source plant.
A dark achene is automatically mature: External appearance should be combined with harvest timing and testing.
evidenceLimits: Pollen longevity and dispersal depend strongly on moisture, temperature, airflow, and handling. Use measured facility or field controls rather than universal distance claims.
